why: Reader only remarks that the order task is fine; all natural orders are accepted.
'Imagine a different past and its result now' describes the structure; a plain situation with 'now' rules out the other options by itself.

fix.q: Choose the correct option: I didn't charge my phone last night, so it's dead now.
fix.why: The condition changes a past event; *would* + base form gives its result now.
fix.why_lv: Nosacījums maina pagātnes notikumu; *would* + pamatforma izsaka tā sekas tagad.

why: Reader 1 only typed two words per gap; the content is the key's. 'd for had in gap 1 is correct and the checker does not add 'd.
Six cards, one possible order, apologise for + -ing: far too easy for B2.2 as evidence.
suggested to meet is the card's typical mistake and the three right sentences use different verbs; reporting-verb patterns are the B2.2 point of this card (EGP B2).
'refused take' is a form nobody writes; replaced by the map's real mistake 'refused that he would'. The task reports meaning (No, I won't = refuse), a B2 reporting-verb point.

wrong: He refused taking another exam.
He refused that he would take another exam.
He refused to taking another exam.

why: Every correct form (-ing, having + 3rd form, that-clause with and without that) is already accepted.
Readers find the only order and call it fine.
'can to meet' and 'can meets' test the modal, not the point (statement order after whether); the wrong options are now all question-order mistakes from the card.

wrong: whether can the supplier meet the deadline
if can the supplier meet the deadline
whether is the supplier able to meet the deadline

why: 'ought to take' and the formal 'are to take' are correct English in statement order.
accept: It is unclear which route we ought to take.
It's unclear which route we ought to take.
It is unclear which route we are to take.
It's unclear which route we are to take.

why: Basic third-conditional form with three options and obvious wrong forms: a B1 point (map c3: B1), far too easy for B2.1 evidence.
'had save' reads as a typo; the mistake B2 learners really make is would in the if-part (card mistake, rules 21 Nov example).

fix.correct: If I would have saved a copy, I wouldn't have lost my work.
fix.why: No *would* in the *if*-part: *If I had saved a copy*.
fix.why_lv: *If* daļā nelieto *would*: *If I had saved a copy*.

why: Basic third-conditional form, three options with obvious wrong forms: B1 point, far too easy for B2.1.
Third conditional rewrite with if and would named: a B1 point. phoned/rung are not added: a rewrite keeps the sentence's own verb.
Basic reported yes/no question with weak wrong forms (could fixed, could to fix): B1 point, far too easy for B2.1.
told me not to + base form is a B1 point (map rep_orders B1); far too easy for B2.1 evidence.
where did I buy is the card's main mistake, still made at B2; the three right sentences are about different things (whether + past perfect, if + could, how long + would).
Both reports are already accepted, but the key also accepts two unnatural fronted orders with a lower-case name ('If I could check the figures, omar asked me.'); they are removed.

answers: Omar asked me to check the figures.
Omar asked me if I could check the figures.
Omar asked me whether I could check the figures.
Omar asked if I could check the figures.
Omar asked whether I could check the figures.
fix.why: A request can be reported as *asked me to check* or *asked me if/whether I could check*.
fix.why_lv: Lūgumu var atstāstīt ar *asked me to check* vai *asked me if/whether I could check*.

why: Readers find the order fine, but the key accepts 'when the storm began for hours we had been hiking', which is not a natural order (rule 4 Nov); removed.

answers: we had been hiking for hours when the storm began
when the storm began we had been hiking for hours
the storm began when we had been hiking for hours
when we had been hiking for hours the storm began
for hours we had been hiking when the storm began
fix.why: *Had been* + *-ing* describes an activity continuing up to a past event.
fix.why_lv: *Had been + -ing* izsaka darbību, kas turpinājās līdz pagātnes notikumam.

why: had been + -ing with a visible result (wet floor, all night) is the B2 point of this card; 'had been leak' is the card's own mistake. Reader 2 finds the level fine.
'd answered is correct and the checker does not add 'd. 'answered' is rejected: the task was rewritten (4 Nov) so that by the time ... so she left early needs had + 3rd form.
Reader 1 is right that 'when she moved for years she had been learning French' is odd; it is not a natural order and is removed from the key.

answers: she had been learning French for years when she moved
when she moved she had been learning French for years
she moved when she had been learning French for years
when she had been learning French for years she moved
for years she had been learning French when she moved
fix.why: *Had been* + *-ing* describes an activity continuing up to a past event.
fix.why_lv: *Had been + -ing* izsaka darbību, kas turpinājās līdz pagātnes notikumam.

why: Reader only calls the instruction fine; would/could/would be able to are all accepted.
Both readers pick the key (would after if). Option A is a correct mixed conditional (card: present quality, past result), so it is rightly one of the correct sentences.
Reader only remarks on meaning; it is the card's present-quality, past-result pattern.
The key is right, but the correct sentence 'Were she less shy...' uses inversion with Were, which the cond_mixed card does not teach (only Had); replaced by a card form.

wrong: Had he trained harder, he would be in the team now.
If she weren't so shy, she would have spoken up at the meeting.
Had they not moved, they would live next door now.

why: Reader only notes the bare instruction; one option is correct.

must may stay or become had to, and to warm up is accepted; 'have to' is rejected by the taught rule (one step back after a past reporting verb, 11 Nov). Reader 2's answer is the key's answer with optional that.
told that without a person is the say/tell point (map: A2, app from B1.1); a B1 point in a B2.1 frame.
no would after as soon as is a good B2.1 point, but 'did landed' and 'would calling' are forms nobody writes; replaced by 'will land' and the card's told-without-a-person mistake.

wrong: My sister said she would call me as soon as she would land.
My sister said she would call me as soon as she will land.
My sister told she would call me as soon as she landed.
fix.why: *will* becomes *would*; after *as soon as* no *would* or *will*: *as soon as she landed*. *tell* needs a person: *told me*.
fix.why_lv: *will* kļūst par *would*; aiz *as soon as* nelieto *would* vai *will*: *as soon as she landed*. Aiz *tell* vajag personu: *told me*.

why: 'mighted' is a form nobody writes; replaced by the card's mistake 'told' without a person.

wrong: The agent told I might need a visa.
The agent said I might to need a visa.
The agent said me I might need a visa.
fix.why: *might* does not change, and the base form follows it. *tell* needs a person (*told me*); *say* takes none, or *to* (*said to me*).
fix.why_lv: *might* nemainās, aiz tā lieto pamatformu. Aiz *tell* vajag personu (*told me*); aiz *say* personu nelieto vai pievieno ar *to* (*said to me*).

why: 'how to starting' and 'how she should starts' are random forms; replaced by card mistakes (do-question order, asked to me). how to in a reported question stays a B2.2 point.

wrong: She asked me how should she start.
She asked me how do I start.
She asked to me how to start.
fix.why: In a reported question the word order is like a statement, with no *do*: *how to start* or *how she should start*. *ask* takes the person without *to*.
fix.why_lv: Atstāstītā jautājumā vārdu secība ir kā apgalvojumā, bez *do*: *how to start* vai *how she should start*. Aiz *ask* personu liek bez *to*.

why: 'ought to' (= should) and the formal 'were to' are correct reports in statement order. 'had to / would have to' are not added: they turn advice into an obligation (do not accept forms that change the meaning).
accept: They asked what time they ought to arrive.
They asked what time they were to arrive.

why: 'asked have the invoices been sent' is the card's mistake type (She asked do I like coffee): learners drop if/whether and keep question order.
'advised to me get' is an unlikely error; replaced by the map's real mistake 'advised to get' (no person).

wrong: She advised me getting a second opinion before the operation.
She suggested me to get a second opinion before the operation.
She advised to get a second opinion before the operation.

why: Reader only notes that urge is stronger than should; the start is given and all forms are accepted.
The key is right, but 'complained about' is not on the rep_verbs card (rule 22 Nov); replaced by a tense mistake in the that-clause. 'complained me that' is on the grammar map's mistake list.

wrong: The client complained that the delivery has been three days late.
The client complained that the delivery had be three days late.
The client complained me that the delivery had been three days late.

why: 'where to going', 'where go we', 'where to we go' are unlikely; replaced by the card's question-order mistake and the map's 'where go'.

wrong: where should we go
where do we go
where go

why: 'using to' names the answer; without it, 'who she should ask' is also correct, so it is accepted and the task checks statement order or question word + to.

fix.q: Join the sentences: She didn't know. Who should she ask?
answers: She didn't know who to ask.
She didn't know whom to ask.
She didn't know who she should ask.
She didn't know whom she should ask.
fix.why: A question inside a sentence: *who to ask* (question word + *to* + base form) or *who she should ask* (statement order).
fix.why_lv: Jautājums teikuma iekšā: *who to ask* (jautājamais vārds + *to* + pamatforma) vai *who she should ask* (apgalvojuma vārdu secība).

why: 'how we do will pay' is a string nobody writes and 'will to pay' tests another point; all wrong options are now question-order mistakes.

wrong: It remains unclear how will we pay for the repairs.
It remains unclear how are we going to pay for the repairs.
It remains unclear how do we pay for the repairs.

why: 'Wh…' is an unclear cue and lets through 'What you decide doesn't matter; ...'. A start that does not contain the answer (I'll support you) makes the -ever clause necessary; every correct ending is accepted.

fix.q: Rewrite as one sentence. Start with *I'll support you*: It doesn't matter what you decide. I'll support you.
answers: I'll support you whatever you decide.
I will support you whatever you decide.
I'll support you no matter what you decide.
I will support you no matter what you decide.
I'll support you whichever way you decide.
I'll support you however you decide.
I'll support you regardless of what you decide.
fix.why: *whatever you decide* = it does not matter what you decide (*no matter what* means the same); no *will* after it.
fix.why_lv: *whatever you decide* nozīmē “lai ko tu izlemtu” (*no matter what* nozīmē to pašu); aiz tā nelieto *will*.

why: Key is right, but 'whichever' is not on the ind_advanced card (whoever, whatever, wherever) and the mistake sentence copies the card example (Whoever finishes first can go home).

fix.correct: Whomever gets home first should start dinner.
wrong: Invite whoever you like to the party.
Whatever happens, stay calm.
Wherever you go, call me first.
fix.why_lv: Darbības vārda *gets* teikuma priekšmets ir *whoever*, nevis *whomever*.

why: Basic second conditional (if + knew): far too easy for B2.1. 'were to know' and 'had known' are rejected: with a state verb and 'right now' they are not natural English.
Basic second conditional, was/were both accepted: far too easy for B2.1.
'might exercise' is correct (card: could or might can replace would) and must be accepted; 'would work out' ignores the verb in brackets. Basic second conditional: practice only at B2.1.

answers: would exercise
'd exercise
might exercise
could exercise
fix.why: The result of an imagined present: *would* (or *could, might*) + base form.

why: Basic third conditional if-part: B1 point, far too easy for B2.1.
'might have helped' is correct (card: could have / might have) and must be accepted. Basic third conditional: practice only at B2.1.

answers: would have helped
'd have helped
might have helped
could have helped
fix.why: The result in an imagined past: *would have* (or *could have, might have*) + 3rd form.
fix.why_lv: Sekas iedomātā pagātnē: *would have* (vai *could have, might have*) + 3. forma.

why: Without the words said, 'was going to send', 'was sending', 'would be sending' are also correct; the quote (allowed pattern, 14 Nov) makes would send the one answer. will to would is a B1 point: practice only.

fix.q: 'I'll send the report tomorrow.' Tom said he ___ the report the next day. (send)

why: Without the words said, 'lived' is a correct report of 'I lived in Riga for two years'. The quote makes had lived / had been living the answer (past perfect in reports: EGP B2); present perfect stays rejected by the taught rule (11 Nov).

fix.q: 'I've lived here for two years.' She told me she ___ there for two years. (live)
fix.why: Reported later: *have lived* becomes *had lived* (or *had been living*).
fix.why_lv: Atstāstot vēlāk, *have lived* kļūst par *had lived* (vai *had been living*).

why: Already practice only. 'am' is rejected by the taught rule (one step back after asked, 11 Nov); 'came' ignores the verb in brackets.
Already practice only. 'have studied / have been studying' are rejected by the taught rule (11 Nov); 'was studying' does not report 'How long have you been studying?'.
'opened' is correct English for a past opening time, but a learner writing it is usually making the backshift the card warns against; a time word (rule 29 Oct) leaves only the habitual present.

fix.q: Could you tell me what time the museum ___ on Sundays? (open)
answers: opens
fix.why: The embedded question has subject before verb and no *does*: *what time the museum opens*.
fix.why_lv: Netiešajā jautājumā teikuma priekšmets ir pirms darbības vārda, un nav *does*: *what time the museum opens*.
